title: The Afternoon Brief: Middle East war reshapes U.S. politics as oil hits $100
dek: Thursday brought military escalation in the Gulf, legal rulings constraining Trump administration actions, and campaign announcements linking the war's outcome to November elections. The common thread: competing timelines, military strikes, court orders, and electoral calendars all colliding at once.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Oil's breach of $100 a barrel and Trump's statement that the Iran war will end after the midterms have tied military conflict directly to electoral politics, reshaping campaign messaging and market expectations for the next eight weeks.
bottom_line: Oil's return to $100 a barrel and Trump's statement tying the Iran war's end to the midterms have collapsed the distance between military conflict and electoral politics. Courts blocked administration actions on immigration data-sharing and redistricting while advancing affirmative action challenges. The coming eight weeks will test whether military escalation persists, whether oil prices hold, and whether campaign promises conditional on Republican November victory shift voter behavior. Watch the September 16 UK extradition deadline for the Tate brothers, continued Gulf military activity, the Missouri contempt hearing outcome, and energy market movement.
body: The picture sharpened Thursday around a single collision: the Iran conflict, now seven months old, is driving oil prices and inflation at a moment when Trump administration officials are campaigning on promises conditional on November victory. Trump told the Republican convention in Dallas on September 9 that the war will end "very shortly after the election," contradicting his earlier prediction of a four-to-five-week conflict and explicitly linking military resolution to electoral outcomes. That statement lands as Brent crude topped $105 per barrel Thursday morning and as the ECB raised interest rates to 2.5% citing Middle East conflict as a driver of persistent inflation into 2027.

The military escalation itself continues on three fronts. Iran fired 20 ballistic missiles at the Al-Azraq airbase in Jordan on September 8-9; Jordanian forces intercepted 18 with no reported casualties. The U.S. military destroyed multiple Iranian tankers in the Gulf of Oman in response. Yemen's Houthi rebels seized the strategic port city of Mocha on September 10, positioning them 75 kilometers from the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most critical shipping chokepoints. Each escalation has tightened supply routes and pushed energy costs higher. Bank of America analysts assess a durable deal unlikely before the November 3 midterms, leaving markets sensitive to further attacks over the next eight weeks.

The oil price shock carries direct political weight. U.S. gasoline averaged $4.22 a gallon on September 9, more than a dollar above prices one year earlier. Diesel reached $5.94, an all-time high. UK petrol hit 166.2p per liter, the highest in four years. The ECB's rate increase reflects the same pressure: headline inflation will not return to target until the first half of 2027, officials stated Thursday, making elevated borrowing costs a fixture through the midterms and beyond.

Courts meanwhile constrained other Trump administration enforcement actions. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia upheld an injunction on September 9 blocking the IRS from sharing taxpayer information with ICE, ruling the data-sharing policy violated federal tax-confidentiality law enacted after Watergate. The IRS had already shared 47,289 taxpayer records before the lower-court block took effect. In Missouri, the state's highest court opened a contempt investigation into Secretary of State Denny Hoskins on September 9 for defying a redistricting ruling, while a federal judge issued a conflicting directive requiring use of the new map. Hoskins is scheduled to appear for a hearing on September 10. The ruling on UC Berkeley Law School's admissions practices represents a different vector: the Justice Department and Education Department jointly found the school deliberately discriminates against white and Asian applicants, with black applicants having 5.8 times higher odds of admission than comparable white applicants in 2025.

Campaign announcements carried stakes beyond individual races. In New Hampshire, Rep. Chris Pappas won the Democratic primary and former Sen. John E. Sununu won the Republican primary on September 9, setting up a closely watched Senate race in November. Trump endorsed Sununu despite Sununu's 2024 op-ed calling Trump a "loser" and his criticism of Trump's tariff policy and the Iran war decision. Democratic Senator John Fetterman appeared in a pre-recorded video at the GOP convention on September 9, calling himself a "commonsense Democrat" and endorsing his Republican colleague Dave McCormick while pledging to work with Trump on steel jobs. Fetterman maintained to CBS News that he will remain a Democrat and vote with his party if it holds or gains Senate control, though polling shows only 22 percent of Pennsylvania Democrats view him favorably while he polls more favorably with Pennsylvania Republicans than McCormick himself. In Rhode Island, former CVS executive Helena Foulkes defeated incumbent Governor Dan McKee in the Democratic primary on September 9, marking the first time in more than 30 years a sitting Rhode Island governor has lost a primary. The race turned on voter anger over McKee's 2023 decision to close the Washington Bridge, which remains under repair three years later.

Trump also announced at the Dallas convention on September 9 that every adult U.S. citizen would receive a $5,000 "dividend" if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November, with no specified funding mechanism or timeline disclosed. Vice President JD Vance suggested the payments could be funded by tariff revenue. Legal experts disagreed on whether the pledge would violate federal laws prohibiting payments intended to influence voting, though all agreed Congress would need to authorize any actual spending.

Administration actions continued on other fronts. The Trump administration proposed changes on September 9 to the 2030 U.S. Census that would exclude undocumented immigrants from the decennial count used for congressional apportionment and eliminate questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Kelly Rogers, who has overseen the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services since May 2026, announced her resignation on September 9 effective September 11, less than a day before her office staff were scheduled to move to the Department of Health and Human Services as part of the administration's effort to dismantle the Education Department.

In international developments unrelated to the Gulf conflict, an Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport on September 8, killing five people in a van and injuring five others. Flight data show pilots attempted to abort the landing before the aircraft overran the runway by approximately 1,300 feet, struck ground crew, breached the airport perimeter, and collided with an SUV on a city street. The NTSB continues investigating what role weather, pilot decisions, or runway safety systems played in the failure to abort in time.

On technology, Apple announced the iPhone Duo on September 9, a foldable device priced at $1,999 with a 7.6-inch internal screen and 5.4-inch external display, marking the company's entry into the foldables market long dominated by Samsung. Preorders begin October 16 with retail availability October 23.

A fire erupted aboard the M/V June Aster ferry off Palawan, Philippines on September 9, leaving at least five confirmed dead and 87 missing as of Thursday morning, with 42 rescued and search operations ongoing.
